title: Email Marketing & Automation
subtitle: Build a consent-based list, reach the inbox and automate emails that people want to read
description:
Email remains one of the most dependable channels for creators, e-commerce brands and service businesses because you own the relationship. This course shows you how to build and use that relationship responsibly and profitably in 2026.

You will grow a list with genuine consent, segment without being invasive, and reach the inbox by configuring **SPF, DKIM and DMARC**, meeting the **Google, Yahoo and Microsoft bulk-sender requirements** (one-click unsubscribe, spam-rate thresholds) and adding **BIMI**. You will learn what Apple Mail Privacy Protection and AI-powered inboxes change, write and design emails (with AI assistance and the right disclosures), and build welcome, abandoned-cart, post-purchase and win-back flows with ready-to-adapt copy. Finally, you will measure revenue per recipient and incrementality, apply CAN-SPAM, GDPR/UK GDPR, PECR and Gulf and Pakistani rules, and extend your programme to **WhatsApp Business and SMS**.

lessons.title: Building a list with consent
lessons.body:
### Why email still matters

Email is an **owned channel**: no algorithm decides whether your subscribers see your posts, and your list stays yours if a social platform changes its rules. For creators, e-commerce brands, coaches and B2B service firms, a healthy list often produces some of the most reliable revenue per unit of effort. But that only holds if people genuinely want your emails.

### Consent first

Build your list on clear, informed permission:

- **Tell people what they will get and how often** ("Weekly tips on freelance pricing, plus occasional offers").
- **Use unticked opt-in boxes** where consent is needed; pre-ticked boxes are not valid consent under the GDPR and UK GDPR.
- **Keep records** of when, where and how each person subscribed.
- **Never buy, rent or scrape lists.** Purchased lists damage deliverability (they often contain spam traps and invalid addresses), break the law in many countries and destroy trust.
- **Consider double opt-in** (a confirmation email before adding someone). It improves list quality and provides proof of consent, at the cost of some sign-ups.

The compliance lesson in this course covers the legal detail by region.

### Lead magnets: give value for the email

A **lead magnet** is something useful offered in exchange for an email address. The best lead magnets are specific, quick to consume and closely related to what you sell.

| Business | Lead magnet idea |
|---|---|
| Freelance designer | "Brand checklist for new restaurants" PDF |
| Skincare brand | Skin-type quiz with personalised routine |
| Accountant (UK) | "Self-assessment deadline calendar" |
| Online Quran or Arabic tutor | Free trial lesson booking plus printable worksheet |
| E-commerce store | Welcome discount or free delivery on first order |
| B2B SaaS | Template, calculator or benchmark report based on real data you own |

Discount-led lead magnets grow lists quickly but can attract bargain hunters. Value-led magnets (guides, tools, quizzes) often attract more engaged subscribers. Many brands use both.

### Where to collect sign-ups

- **Website forms:** homepage section, blog post footers, dedicated landing pages.
- **Pop-ups:** use carefully. Show after engagement (for example scroll depth or exit intent), make them easy to close and avoid intrusive mobile pop-ups that cover content.
- **Checkout:** with a separate, optional marketing opt-in.
- **Social media:** link in bio to a landing page; lead ads on Meta, TikTok or LinkedIn with clear consent wording.
- **Events and in-store:** QR codes to a sign-up page (rather than paper forms that must be typed up).
- **Content upgrades:** a downloadable extra relevant to a specific blog post.

### Designing a high-converting sign-up form

- A clear headline stating the benefit.
- As few fields as possible (email and perhaps first name). Every extra field reduces sign-ups.
- A consent statement and link to your privacy notice.
- A specific button ("Send me the checklist" rather than "Submit").
- Social proof if genuine ("Join 3,000+ freelancers" only if true).

### WhatsApp and SMS as companions

In Pakistan and the Gulf, WhatsApp is often as important as email. Treat it with the same consent discipline: explicit opt-in to marketing messages, clear expectations, easy opt-out and respect for WhatsApp Business policies. Email and messaging can work together (for example email for detailed content, WhatsApp for time-sensitive updates the subscriber asked for).

### Worked example

A Lahore-based online clothing store adds:

1. A value-led quiz ("Find your Eid outfit style") with results emailed.
2. A 10% first-order code offered in an exit-intent pop-up on desktop and a small banner on mobile.
3. An unticked marketing checkbox at checkout.

All sign-ups receive a double opt-in email. The store tracks which source each subscriber came from to compare engagement later.

### Common mistakes

- Buying or scraping email lists.
- Pre-ticked consent boxes or hidden consent.
- Vague promises ("Subscribe to our newsletter").
- Long forms asking for unnecessary data.

### Hands-on: sign-up form and confirmation email you can adapt

**Form copy (e-commerce example):**

```text
Headline:   Get the Summer Skin Routine (free 3-step guide)
Sub-line:   Plus new-product news and occasional offers. About one email a week.
Field:      Email address   [ you@example.com ]
Checkbox:   [ ] Yes, email me the guide and GlowLab news and offers. I can
                unsubscribe anytime. See our Privacy Notice.
Button:     Send me the guide
Microcopy:  We never sell your data.
```

The box is **unticked**; the form records timestamp, source (page URL or pop-up ID), IP address and the consent wording version shown.

**Double opt-in (confirmation) email:**

```text
Subject:  Confirm to get your Summer Skin Routine
Preview:  One click and the guide is on its way
Body:     Hi there, you asked for our 3-step Summer Skin Routine.
          Please confirm your email so we can send it:
          [Confirm my email]
          Didn't sign up? Ignore this email and you won't hear from us.
          – Hira, founder of GlowLab
```

Send it instantly, keep it short and put the button above the fold. Track the **confirmation rate**; if it is low, check spam placement and whether the email arrives quickly.

### Worked example 2: a Riyadh fitness studio

A women-only fitness studio in Riyadh collects sign-ups with a QR code at reception linking to a bilingual (Arabic/English) form offering a "7-day beginner plan". The form asks for email and preferred language only, with a clear consent line and a separate, optional checkbox for WhatsApp updates. The welcome email arrives in the chosen language within a minute. Because consent for email and WhatsApp is collected separately, the studio can honour each channel's opt-out independently.

### How to measure success

| Metric | Formula | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Form conversion rate | Sign-ups ÷ form views | Offer and form quality |
| Confirmation rate (double opt-in) | Confirmed ÷ sign-ups | Deliverability and intent |
| Net list growth rate (monthly) | (New confirmed − unsubscribes − bounces − complaints) ÷ list size at start | Overall list health |
| First-30-day click rate by source | Unique clicks ÷ delivered, per acquisition source | Which sources bring engaged people |

Compare sources after 30 days: a source that brings many sign-ups but few clicks (typical of giveaways) may be hurting you.

video.script: Here's the most important idea in email marketing: your list is only as valuable as the permission behind it. Email is an owned channel. No algorithm decides whether your subscribers see your message, and your list stays yours even if a social platform changes its rules overnight. But that power only works when people genuinely want to hear from you. So build your list with consent. Tell people exactly what they'll receive and how often. Use unticked boxes where consent is required, keep a record of when and how each person signed up, and never, ever buy a list. Purchased lists are full of people who never asked for your email, and often spam traps too. They'll damage your sender reputation and can break the law. Instead, earn sign-ups with a lead magnet: something specific and useful. A checklist, a quiz, a template, a free trial lesson or a welcome offer. Keep your form short, just an email and maybe a first name, and make the button say what they'll get, like "Send me the checklist". And if you use WhatsApp or SMS alongside email, apply the same rules: clear opt-in, clear expectations, and an easy way out. In the rest of this course, you'll turn that permission into relevant, well-timed messages that people look forward to opening.

lessons.title: Segmentation and personalisation
lessons.body:
### Relevance drives results

Sending the same email to everyone is simple but blunt. Subscribers who receive irrelevant emails ignore them, unsubscribe or mark them as spam, which hurts deliverability for everyone on your list. **Segmentation** means dividing your list into groups that receive different messages; **personalisation** means adapting content to the individual.

### Data you can segment on

| Data type | Examples | How you get it |
|---|---|---|
| **Declared (zero-party)** | Interests, preferences, skin type, budget, language | Sign-up forms, quizzes, preference centres |
| **Behavioural** | Emails opened or clicked, pages viewed, products browsed | Email platform and website tracking (with consent where required) |
| **Transactional** | Purchases, order value, frequency, last purchase date | E-commerce or CRM integration |
| **Lifecycle stage** | New subscriber, first-time buyer, repeat customer, lapsed | Combination of the above |
| **Location and language** | Country, city, preferred language | Forms, store data |

Only collect data you will use and that your privacy notice covers.

### High-impact starter segments

1. **New subscribers** (joined in the last 30 days) – still forming an opinion; send onboarding content.
2. **Engaged subscribers** (clicked in the last 60–90 days) – your most responsive audience.
3. **Unengaged subscribers** (no clicks in many months) – candidates for re-engagement or suppression.
4. **Customers vs non-customers** – different messages and offers.
5. **Repeat or high-value customers** – loyalty perks, early access.
6. **Interest segments** – for example "menswear" vs "womenswear", or "beginner" vs "advanced".
7. **Language or region** – Arabic and English versions for Gulf audiences; UK vs US spelling, currency and holidays.

### The RFM model for e-commerce

**RFM** scores customers on:

- **Recency:** how recently they bought.
- **Frequency:** how often they buy.
- **Monetary value:** how much they spend.

Customers who bought recently, often and with high spend are your champions; those who used to buy often but have not recently are at risk. Many email platforms calculate RFM-style segments automatically.

### A note on open-based segmentation

Since Apple's Mail Privacy Protection (introduced in 2021), emails opened in Apple Mail can be pre-loaded, which records an "open" even if the person never read it. This inflates open rates and makes "opened in the last 30 days" segments unreliable. Use **clicks, site visits and purchases** as stronger engagement signals.

### Personalisation that helps, not creeps

Useful personalisation:

- First name in the greeting (with a sensible fallback like "Hi there" when the name is missing).
- Product recommendations based on browsing or purchase history.
- Content blocks that change by interest or location (dynamic content).
- Send-time optimisation where the platform supports it.
- Language and currency matching.

Avoid personalisation that feels invasive ("We noticed you looked at this item 7 times at 2am") or that reveals sensitive information. Never infer or reference sensitive characteristics such as health or religion without explicit, appropriate permission.

### Preference centres

A **preference centre** lets subscribers choose topics and frequency instead of unsubscribing completely. Offer options such as "weekly digest only", "offers only" or "pause for a month" (useful around exams, Ramadan or busy seasons). This keeps more subscribers and improves relevance.

### Worked example

A UK and UAE online bookstore segments by:

- **Language:** English or Arabic newsletters.
- **Genre interests:** from a sign-up quiz (fiction, business, children's).
- **Lifecycle:** new subscribers, first-time buyers, repeat buyers, lapsed buyers.

The weekly newsletter uses dynamic blocks to show each reader's preferred genres, and repeat buyers get early access to signed editions. Unengaged subscribers move to a monthly digest before any suppression.

### Common mistakes

- Blasting every campaign to the whole list.
- Relying on opens as the main engagement signal.
- Collecting data you never use.
- Personalisation errors like "Hi {FIRST_NAME}" (test merge tags and fallbacks).

### Hands-on: segment definitions you can build in any ESP

Most email platforms (Klaviyo, Mailchimp, Brevo, HubSpot and others) let you build segments from conditions. Write them in plain language first, then build:

```text
ENGAGED 90D      Clicked any email in last 90 days OR placed order in last 90 days
                 OR (signed up in last 30 days)
UNENGAGED 180D   Received >= 10 emails AND no clicks in 180 days AND no orders in 365 days
NEW CUSTOMERS    Placed exactly 1 order, first order in last 60 days
REPEAT / VIP     Placed >= 3 orders OR total spend in top 10% of customers
AT RISK          Placed >= 2 orders AND last order > 1.5 x their usual reorder gap
BROWSED NOT BOUGHT  Viewed product in category X in last 14 days AND no order in 14 days
LANGUAGE = AR    Preferred language (from form or site) = Arabic
```

Use **clicks and orders**, not opens, as engagement signals (the next module explains why opens are unreliable).

### Hands-on: RFM scores in Google Sheets

Export customers with columns: customer_id (A), days since last order (B), number of orders (C), total spend (D). Score each 1–5 by quintile:

```text
R score E2: =6-MATCH(PERCENTRANK.INC($B$2:$B$1000,B2),{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8})
F score F2: =MATCH(PERCENTRANK.INC($C$2:$C$1000,C2),{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8})
M score G2: =MATCH(PERCENTRANK.INC($D$2:$D$1000,D2),{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8})
Segment H2: =IF(AND(E2>=4,F2>=4),"Champion",IF(AND(E2<=2,F2>=4),"At risk",
             IF(E2>=4,"Recent",IF(E2<=2,"Lapsing","Steady"))))
```

(Recency is inverted: fewer days since the last order scores higher.) Many platforms calculate similar segments automatically; the sheet helps you understand and check them. Use customer IDs, not names or emails, in any file you share.

### Worked example 2: a Karachi electronics retailer

The retailer used to send every promotion to its whole list of 60,000. It creates four segments: engaged buyers (weekly offers), engaged non-buyers (buying guides and reviews), at-risk customers (a service check-in and accessory offer) and unengaged subscribers (monthly digest, then re-engagement). Sends to the unengaged group fall sharply, complaint rates drop and revenue per recipient rises on every campaign – with fewer emails sent.

### How to measure success

- **Revenue or clicks per recipient by segment**, compared with the old whole-list sends.
- **Share of the list that is engaged** (clicked or bought in 90 days) trending up.
- **Unsubscribe and complaint rates** falling on promotional sends.

lessons.title: Authentication: SPF, DKIM and DMARC
lessons.body:
### Deliverability is the foundation

An email that lands in spam, or is rejected, earns nothing. **Deliverability** is the ability to reach the inbox. It depends on three things: **authentication** (proving you are who you say you are), **reputation** (how recipients and mailbox providers judge your sending) and **content and engagement** (whether people want your email).

### The three authentication standards

**SPF (Sender Policy Framework)**
A DNS TXT record listing which servers are allowed to send email for your domain. Example:

```
v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net ~all
```

- One SPF record per domain (combine includes into one record).
- There is a limit of 10 DNS lookups; too many includes can break SPF.

**DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)**
A digital signature added to each email, verified with a public key published in your DNS. It proves the message was authorised by the domain and not altered in transit. Your email platform provides the DKIM records to add. Use a key length of at least 1024 bits (2048 recommended where supported).

**DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance)**
A DNS policy that tells receivers what to do when an email fails authentication, and where to send reports. Example:

```
v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com
```

- **p=none:** monitor only.
- **p=quarantine:** send failing mail to spam.
- **p=reject:** block failing mail.

DMARC requires **alignment**: the domain in the visible "From" address must match (align with) the domain authenticated by SPF or DKIM. This is why you should send from your own domain with custom DKIM, not a platform's shared domain.

### Mailbox provider requirements

Since 2024, Google and Yahoo have required bulk senders (Google defines this as sending close to 5,000 or more messages a day to Gmail accounts) to:

- Authenticate with **SPF and DKIM**, and publish a **DMARC** policy (at least p=none) with alignment.
- Offer **one-click unsubscribe** in marketing messages (the List-Unsubscribe header) and honour unsubscribes within two days.
- Keep reported **spam complaint rates low** – Google advises staying below 0.1% and never reaching 0.3% or higher.

Microsoft introduced similar requirements for high-volume senders to Outlook.com addresses in 2025. Even if you send less, following these rules is best practice and protects your domain.

### Setting it up: a practical sequence

1. **Use a domain you control** (for example `news.yourbrand.com` or `yourbrand.com`), never a free Gmail or Yahoo address as the sender for bulk email.
2. **Add SPF** including your email platform.
3. **Add DKIM** records supplied by your email platform.
4. **Add DMARC with p=none** and a reporting address; use a DMARC reporting tool to read the reports.
5. **Review reports** for a few weeks to find legitimate services failing authentication (for example your invoicing tool or CRM).
6. **Tighten gradually** to p=quarantine, then p=reject, once all legitimate sources pass.
7. Consider a **subdomain** for marketing email to separate its reputation from your team's everyday email.

### Warming up a new domain or IP

Mailbox providers are cautious with senders they do not know. When starting with a new domain or dedicated IP, **warm up**: start by sending to your most engaged subscribers in smaller volumes, then increase gradually over several weeks. Sudden large sends from a new domain look like spam behaviour.

### Tools to check

- Your email platform's domain authentication page.
- DNS lookup and DMARC checking tools.
- **Google Postmaster Tools** for spam rate and authentication data at Gmail.
- **Microsoft SNDS** for Outlook-related data.

### Worked example

A Dubai events company sends newsletters from `info@company.ae` via an email platform without custom DKIM. Gmail users see "via platform.com" and many emails go to spam. The team adds SPF and DKIM for the platform, publishes DMARC with p=none, discovers their ticketing tool also sends as the domain and authenticates it too, then moves to p=quarantine after a month. Inbox placement and click rates improve.

### Common mistakes

- Multiple SPF records on one domain.
- Sending from a free mailbox address.
- Jumping straight to p=reject and blocking legitimate email.
- Blasting a new domain with a large list on day one.

### Hands-on: a complete DNS record set (example)

For a brand sending staff email through Google Workspace and marketing email through an email platform on the subdomain `news.example.com` (values are illustrative – always copy the exact records your providers give you):

```text
; SPF for the root domain (staff email)
example.com.            TXT   "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all"

; SPF for the marketing subdomain (your ESP gives the include or a CNAME)
news.example.com.       TXT   "v=spf1 include:spf.your-esp.example ~all"

; DKIM – usually CNAMEs pointing to keys your providers host and rotate
google._domainkey.example.com.   TXT    "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkq..."
esp1._domainkey.news.example.com. CNAME esp1.dkim.your-esp.example.

; DMARC – start with monitoring, reports to a mailbox or reporting service
_dmarc.example.com.     TXT   "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com; adkim=r; aspf=r; fo=1"

; Later, once reports are clean (applies to subdomains too unless sp= is set)
_dmarc.example.com.     TXT   "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com"
_dmarc.example.com.     TXT   "v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com"
```

Key tags: `p` = policy for the domain; `sp` = policy for subdomains; `rua` = where aggregate reports go; `adkim`/`aspf` = relaxed (`r`) or strict (`s`) alignment; `pct` = percentage of failing mail the policy applies to (use it to phase in quarantine). Only one DMARC record and one SPF record may exist per name.

### Check your records from a terminal

```bash
dig +short TXT example.com | grep spf1
dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com
dig +short TXT google._domainkey.example.com
# Windows PowerShell alternative:
# Resolve-DnsName -Type TXT _dmarc.example.com
```

Then send a test email to a Gmail account, open it, choose **Show original**, and confirm **SPF: PASS, DKIM: PASS, DMARC: PASS**.

### Reading DMARC reports

Aggregate (`rua`) reports are XML files listing every source that sent mail using your domain, how many messages, and whether SPF and DKIM passed and aligned. Reading raw XML is painful; use a DMARC reporting service or your email platform's DMARC dashboard. Look for:

- **Legitimate sources failing** (your CRM, invoicing tool, helpdesk) → authenticate them.
- **Unknown sources** sending as you → possible spoofing; moving to `p=reject` protects you.

### Worked example 2: a Lahore Shopify brand

A Lahore brand uses Google Workspace, Shopify order emails and Klaviyo for marketing. It adds Klaviyo's branded sending domain (`send.brand.pk`) with its DKIM and SPF records, turns on Shopify's sender domain authentication, and publishes DMARC at `p=none` with a reporting service. Reports show a courier-tracking tool sending as the domain without DKIM; the team configures it. After four weeks of clean reports, DMARC moves to `p=quarantine; pct=25`, then 100%, then `p=reject`. Gmail placement improves and spoofed "order update" scams using the brand's domain are blocked.

### How to measure success

- 100% of legitimate mail passing SPF or DKIM **with alignment** in DMARC reports.
- DMARC at `p=quarantine` or `p=reject` (also required for BIMI – next lesson).
- Authentication shown as passing in Google Postmaster Tools, with no unexplained sources in reports.

lessons.title: Google, Yahoo and Microsoft sender rules, one-click unsubscribe and BIMI
lessons.body:
### The rules changed – and are now enforced

Since February 2024, Gmail and Yahoo have required **bulk senders** to meet stricter standards, and Gmail stepped up enforcement from November 2025 with temporary and permanent rejections of non-compliant traffic. Microsoft introduced similar rules for high-volume senders to Outlook.com, Hotmail and Live addresses, rejecting non-compliant mail from 5 May 2025. If you send marketing email at any scale, treat these as the minimum standard.

### Who counts as a bulk sender?

- **Gmail:** a sender that has sent close to **5,000 or more messages in a day** to personal Gmail accounts. Google says that once you reach this level, you are treated as a bulk sender permanently.
- **Microsoft:** domains sending **over 5,000 emails a day** to Outlook.com consumer addresses.
- **Yahoo:** applies similar bulk-sender standards; its requirements page does not rely on a single public threshold for all rules.

Small senders should follow the same practices anyway – they are what good deliverability looks like.

### The requirements side by side (as of September 2026 – check each provider's page)

| Requirement | Gmail (bulk) | Yahoo (bulk) | Microsoft (high-volume) |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPF **and** DKIM | Required | Required | Required |
| DMARC policy (at least `p=none`) | Required, with From-domain alignment (SPF or DKIM) | Required | Required, aligned with SPF or DKIM |
| One-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058) for marketing | Required, plus a visible unsubscribe link | Required | Recommended: clear, easy unsubscribe |
| Honour unsubscribes | Within 48 hours | Within 2 days | Promptly |
| Spam complaint rate | Keep below 0.1%; never reach 0.3% | Keep below 0.3% | Keep lists clean |
| Other | Valid forward and reverse DNS, TLS, RFC 5322-compliant messages | Valid DNS and standards compliance | Valid From/Reply-To, list hygiene |

Microsoft rejects non-compliant messages with an error along the lines of `550 5.7.515 Access denied, sending domain ... does not meet the required authentication level`. Gmail's user-reported spam rate is visible in **Google Postmaster Tools**; if it exceeds 0.3%, Google says you lose eligibility for its mitigation help until you have stayed below 0.3% for seven consecutive days.

### One-click unsubscribe: what it actually is

"One-click unsubscribe" means mailbox providers can show their own **Unsubscribe** button next to your sender name, and a single click unsubscribes the person without visiting a page. It works through two email headers defined in RFC 8058:

```text
List-Unsubscribe: <https://example.com/u/abc123>, <mailto:unsubscribe@example.com?subject=unsubscribe>
List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click
```

- The HTTPS URL must accept a **POST** request and unsubscribe the recipient immediately – no login, no confirmation page.
- Both headers must be covered by your **DKIM signature**.
- Keep a **visible unsubscribe link** in the email body too.

Most reputable email platforms add these headers automatically when you use their unsubscribe feature. If you send from your own system, implement them yourself. A minimal handler (Python/Flask, illustrative):

```python
from flask import Flask, request, abort

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.post("/u/<token>")
def one_click_unsubscribe(token):
    # Body will be "List-Unsubscribe=One-Click" for RFC 8058 requests
    subscriber = lookup_subscriber_by_token(token)   # your data layer
    if subscriber is None:
        abort(404)
    suppress_everywhere(subscriber.id, reason="one_click")  # email + synced tools
    return "", 200
```

### BIMI: your logo in the inbox

**BIMI (Brand Indicators for Message Identification)** lets supporting mailbox providers show your verified logo next to your emails. It rewards strong authentication and helps recognition.

Requirements:

1. **DMARC at enforcement:** `p=quarantine` or `p=reject`, applied to 100% of mail (no reduced `pct`).
2. **A logo in SVG Tiny Portable/Secure (SVG Tiny PS)** format, square, hosted over HTTPS.
3. **A mark certificate** from an authorised certificate authority:
   - **VMC (Verified Mark Certificate):** requires a registered trademark; enables logo display and, in Gmail, a blue verified checkmark; also used by Apple Mail.
   - **CMC (Common Mark Certificate):** no trademark needed, but the logo must have been in use for at least 12 months; Gmail supports it for logo display (without the checkmark).
4. **A BIMI DNS record:**

```text
default._bimi.example.com.  TXT  "v=BIMI1; l=https://example.com/brand/logo.svg; a=https://example.com/brand/vmc.pem"
```

Support differs by mailbox provider and changes over time – check current support before promising a logo in every inbox. Certificates are paid, annual products; budget for them like any brand-protection cost.

### Worked example: a UK retailer's compliance sprint

Illustrative. A Manchester fashion retailer sends 40,000 emails a week. Google Postmaster Tools shows a spam rate around 0.25% and some rejections after enforcement tightens. The sprint: (1) confirm SPF, DKIM and aligned DMARC for its email platform and for its transactional provider; (2) switch on the platform's one-click unsubscribe and remove the "log in to manage preferences" requirement; (3) suppress subscribers with no clicks or orders in 12 months after a re-engagement series; (4) reduce frequency for low-engagement segments. Within weeks, spam rate drops below 0.1%, rejections stop, and the retailer moves DMARC to `p=reject` and applies for a VMC for BIMI.

### Worked example 2: a Dubai B2B newsletter under the threshold

A Dubai consultancy sends 1,500 newsletters a month – far below bulk thresholds. It still sets up SPF, DKIM, DMARC and one-click unsubscribe because the same filters judge all senders, and because clients' corporate mail systems increasingly check DMARC. Its newsletter now lands reliably in partners' inboxes.

### Common mistakes

- Unsubscribe links that require a login or several steps.
- DKIM not covering the List-Unsubscribe headers when self-hosting.
- Processing unsubscribes weekly in a batch.
- Assuming "we're under 5,000" means the rules do not matter.
- Starting BIMI with DMARC at `p=none`.

### How to measure success

- Google Postmaster Tools: spam rate consistently **below 0.1%**, authentication passing, compliance status healthy.
- Yahoo Sender Hub and Microsoft SNDS data reviewed monthly.
- Unsubscribes processed within 48 hours (ideally instantly) across all tools.
- BIMI logo showing in supported inboxes after DMARC reaches enforcement.

lessons.title: Bounces, complaints and list hygiene
lessons.body:
### Reputation is earned per send

Mailbox providers watch how recipients react to your email. Signals that hurt reputation include **bounces, spam complaints, spam trap hits and low engagement**. Signals that help include opens (where measurable), clicks, replies, moving emails out of spam and adding you to contacts. List hygiene is the routine work that keeps these signals healthy.

### Bounces

A **bounce** is an email that could not be delivered.

- **Hard bounce:** permanent failure – the address does not exist or the domain is invalid. Remove hard-bounced addresses immediately (most platforms suppress them automatically).
- **Soft bounce:** temporary failure – mailbox full, server busy, message too large. Platforms usually retry; repeated soft bounces over several sends should be suppressed.

A high bounce rate usually means old, purchased or mistyped data. Common causes include typos at sign-up (for example "gmial.com"). Real-time email validation at the form and double opt-in reduce them.

### Spam complaints

A complaint happens when a recipient clicks "Report spam". Complaints are one of the strongest negative signals. Common causes:

- People do not remember signing up (long gaps between sign-up and first email).
- Emails are too frequent or not what was promised.
- The unsubscribe link is hard to find, so "Report spam" is easier.
- The list includes people who never consented.

To reduce complaints:

- Send a welcome email immediately after sign-up.
- Make the sender name recognisable and consistent.
- Keep frequency aligned with what you promised.
- Put a clear unsubscribe link in every email and support one-click unsubscribe.
- Sign up to **feedback loops** where available (your email platform typically handles these) so complainers are suppressed automatically.

### Spam traps

**Spam traps** are addresses used by mailbox providers and anti-spam organisations to catch poor practices.

- **Pristine traps:** addresses never used by a real person – they appear on scraped or purchased lists.
- **Recycled traps:** old abandoned addresses reactivated as traps – they catch senders who never remove inactive subscribers.
- **Typo traps:** common misspellings of real domains.

Hitting traps can cause blocklisting. The cure is prevention: consent-based collection, validation and regular removal of long-term inactive addresses.

### Engagement-based sunsetting

Subscribers who have not engaged for a long time drag down reputation. A **sunset policy** handles them:

1. Define inactivity (for example no clicks in 6 months and no purchases in 12 months – choose thresholds that fit your sending frequency and sales cycle).
2. Send a **re-engagement** sequence (covered in the automation module) asking if they still want to hear from you.
3. Suppress those who still do not engage. They can resubscribe any time.

A smaller, engaged list almost always outperforms a large, unengaged one in both inbox placement and revenue per email.

### Monitoring dashboard

| Metric | What to watch |
|---|---|
| Hard bounce rate | Should be very low; spikes point to bad data sources |
| Spam complaint rate | Keep below 0.1% (Gmail); never approach 0.3%; investigate any spike immediately |
| Unsubscribe rate | Rising rates suggest frequency or relevance problems |
| Click rate by segment | Declining engagement predicts deliverability problems |
| Google Postmaster Tools | Spam rate, domain reputation and authentication at Gmail |
| Blocklist checks | Occasional checks with a reputable blocklist lookup |

### Content factors (smaller but real)

- Avoid misleading subject lines and excessive capitals or symbols.
- Keep a healthy text-to-image balance; image-only emails are harder to read and filter.
- Use reputable link destinations and avoid URL shorteners known for abuse.
- Include a plain-text version (most platforms generate one).

### Worked example (illustrative)

A US-based creator's list of 40,000 has a 0.4% complaint rate and falling Gmail placement. Investigation: 15,000 subscribers came from a giveaway three years ago and have not clicked in over a year. She sends a three-email re-engagement series, suppresses about 11,000 who do not respond, moves weekly emails to a clear schedule and adds one-click unsubscribe. Complaint rates fall below 0.1% and click rates per email rise.

### Common mistakes

- Keeping hard bounces on the list.
- Never removing inactive subscribers.
- Hiding the unsubscribe link.
- Long gaps between sign-up and first email.

### Reading bounce codes

Bounce messages include SMTP status codes. A few you will see often:

| Code (example) | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `5.1.1` | Mailbox does not exist | Hard bounce – suppress immediately |
| `5.7.x` (for example `5.7.26`, `5.7.515`) | Rejected for policy or authentication reasons | Fix SPF/DKIM/DMARC or content policy; do not simply retry |
| `4.2.2` | Mailbox full | Soft bounce – retry; suppress after repeated failures |
| `4.7.x` | Temporarily deferred (rate limiting, reputation) | Slow down, check reputation and engagement |

Codes starting with **5** are permanent; **4** are temporary. Your email platform classifies most of them automatically – but a sudden wave of `5.7.x` rejections is an authentication or reputation emergency, not a list problem.

### Hands-on: a sunset policy and re-engagement series

**Policy (adapt thresholds to your send frequency and buying cycle):**

```text
Inactive = received >= 8 emails AND no clicks in 180 days AND no orders in 365 days
           AND subscribed > 90 days ago
Step 1: remove from regular campaigns; enter 3-email re-engagement flow
Step 2: anyone who clicks -> back to "engaged"; offer preference centre
Step 3: no click after final email + 7 days -> suppress (do not delete consent record)
Review: monthly; report number sunset and any change in spam rate / placement
```

**Re-engagement copy:**

```text
Email 1  Subject: Still want to hear from us?
         Body: It's been a while. We don't want to crowd your inbox. Here's what's
         new [3 bullets]. Want to keep getting our emails? [Yes, keep me subscribed]
Email 2  Subject: Pick what you'd like (or less often)
         Body: Choose topics or switch to a monthly digest. [Update my preferences]
Email 3  Subject: We'll stop emailing you soon
         Body: Unless you click below, this is our last email. No hard feelings –
         you can re-subscribe anytime. [Keep me on the list]
```

No guilt-tripping, no fake urgency, and a clear unsubscribe link in every email.

### Feedback loops and monitoring tools

- **Google Postmaster Tools:** spam rate, authentication and delivery errors for Gmail.
- **Yahoo Sender Hub:** sender information and Yahoo's complaint feedback loop.
- **Microsoft SNDS and JMRP:** data and complaint reports for Outlook.com traffic.

Most email platforms process feedback-loop complaints automatically by suppressing the complainer; confirm yours does.

### Worked example 2: a Pakistani e-commerce brand after a sale season

After an 11.11 and White Friday push, a Karachi store sees Gmail spam rate rise to 0.2% and more `4.7.x` deferrals. Investigation: sends to the whole list three times a day, including 70,000 addresses from an old contest. Fixes: frequency caps (one promotional email a day maximum), segment-based sending, the sunset policy above and a pause on the contest segment pending re-engagement. Deferrals clear and spam rate returns below 0.1% within weeks.

lessons.title: Apple Mail Privacy Protection, inbox tabs and AI-powered inboxes
lessons.body:
### The inbox is no longer a simple list

Three changes reshaped what happens after your email is delivered:

1. **Privacy features** (above all Apple Mail Privacy Protection) made opens unreliable.
2. **Sorting** (Gmail tabs, Apple Mail categories, subscription-management views) decides where your email sits and how easy it is to leave.
3. **AI features** in Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail summarise, prioritise and sometimes replace your preview text.

### Apple Mail Privacy Protection (MPP)

Introduced with iOS 15 and macOS Monterey in 2021, MPP lets Apple Mail users hide their activity. When enabled, Apple **pre-loads remote content (including tracking pixels) through proxy servers**, often soon after delivery, whether or not the person reads the email. Consequences:

- **Opens are inflated** for Apple Mail users – an "open" may be a machine fetch.
- **IP-based location and device data** from opens are unreliable (they reflect Apple's proxies).
- **Open-based automations misfire:** "send reminder if not opened", "resend to non-openers" and open-based send-time optimisation lose accuracy.
- **Live content** (countdown timers, real-time stock) may render at fetch time rather than read time.

MPP applies to the Apple Mail app, regardless of which email account (Gmail, Outlook, iCloud) the person uses in it. Separately, iCloud+ **Hide My Email** gives people relay addresses – treat them as normal addresses; they forward to real inboxes.

### What to do about it

| Old practice | Better practice |
|---|---|
| Engagement = opened in last 30 days | Engagement = clicked, visited the site or bought in 60–180 days |
| Subject-line tests judged on opens | Judge on clicks, conversions or revenue per recipient |
| "Resend to non-openers" | Resend (sparingly) to non-clickers of a high-value message, or skip |
| Open rate as the headline KPI | Click rate, conversion rate, revenue per recipient, unsubscribe and complaint rates |
| Sunset on no opens | Sunset on no clicks and no purchases |

Many email platforms now flag or filter **machine or privacy-proxy opens** in reports; use those filtered numbers if available, and still treat opens as directional.

### Where your email lands: tabs, categories and subscription views

- **Gmail tabs:** most marketing email lands in the **Promotions** tab – normal, and people do shop there. Do not use tricks to force Primary; relevance and engagement matter more. Gmail can show deal annotations (such as a discount code or expiry) in Promotions if you add the supported markup – check Google's current documentation.
- **Apple Mail categories:** newer versions of Apple Mail on iPhone sort mail into categories such as Primary, Transactions, Updates and Promotions.
- **Subscription management:** Gmail offers a view listing senders people are subscribed to with one-tap unsubscribe, and providers surface unsubscribe buttons near the sender name. Making leaving easy for uninterested people protects your reputation – which is why the one-click rules exist.

### AI in the inbox

Gmail (with Gemini), Outlook (with Copilot) and Apple Mail (with Apple Intelligence, on supported devices) can **summarise emails**, highlight priority messages and suggest replies. Practical implications:

- **Front-load the point.** Put the key message, offer and deadline in live text in the first lines, because a summary may be what the reader sees instead of your preview text.
- **Avoid image-only emails** – summaries and screen readers cannot read text baked into images.
- **Be clear, not clever.** Vague teasers summarise badly; specific facts summarise well.
- **Consistency beats tricks.** Hidden text meant to steer AI summaries is deceptive and risky.

### Hands-on: an MPP-proof metrics and automation audit

```text
1. Reports: switch dashboard headline KPI from open rate to click rate and revenue per recipient.
2. Segments: rebuild "engaged" on clicks/visits/orders (see Segmentation lesson).
3. Automations: list every flow condition using "opened"; replace with "clicked" or time-based logic.
4. Tests: change A/B winner criteria from opens to clicks or revenue per recipient.
5. Content: check the first 2 lines of your last 5 campaigns - do they state the point in live text?
6. Live content: if using countdown timers, add the deadline in text too.
```

### Worked example: a UK subscription box

Illustrative. The company's "engaged" segment (opened in 30 days) had grown to 85% of the list, yet revenue per email was falling. Filtering out privacy-proxy opens showed true engagement was far lower. They rebuilt engagement on clicks and orders, cut sends to the rest, changed subject-line tests to judge on revenue per recipient and rewrote email openings to state the offer in the first sentence. Complaints fell and revenue per recipient rose.

### Worked example 2: an Arabic-language newsletter in Riyadh

A Riyadh publisher notices AI summaries of its long Arabic newsletter were vague. It adds a three-bullet "In this issue" section in live text at the top and uses clear, specific headings. Summaries and screen readers now describe the newsletter accurately, and click rate on the lead story rises.

### How to measure success

- No open-based conditions left in flows, segments or test criteria.
- Headline KPIs: click rate, conversion rate, revenue per recipient, unsubscribe and spam rate.
- The first two lines of every campaign state the point in live text.

lessons.title: Email copywriting that gets clicks
lessons.body:
### The job of each part

- **Sender name:** earns recognition and trust. Use a consistent, recognisable name ("Amna from Leaf & Loom" or "Leaf & Loom").
- **Subject line:** earns the open.
- **Preview text (preheader):** supports the subject line and adds a reason to open.
- **Body:** delivers value and leads to one main action.
- **Call to action (CTA):** earns the click.

### Subject lines

Principles:

- **Clarity beats cleverness.** The reader should know what is inside.
- **Specificity:** "3 invoice templates for freelancers" beats "Useful resources".
- **Curiosity with honesty:** "The pricing mistake I made for two years" works only if the email delivers.
- **Length:** many inboxes show roughly 30–50 characters on mobile; front-load key words.
- **Personalisation:** first names or location can help, but do not overuse them.
- **Avoid** misleading "RE:" or "FWD:" tricks, fake urgency, excessive capitals and emoji overload. Deceptive subject lines breach CAN-SPAM in the US and erode trust everywhere.

Subject line formulas:

| Formula | Example |
|---|---|
| How-to | How to price your first logo project |
| Number | 5 Ramadan recipes ready in 20 minutes |
| Question | Still chasing late invoices? |
| News/announcement | New: Arabic calligraphy course starts Monday |
| Benefit | Your weekend sorted: 3 easy day trips from Riyadh |
| Personal story | I almost quit freelancing last year |

### Preview text

Use the preview text to extend the subject line, not repeat it. If you leave it blank, inboxes may show "View in browser" or other boilerplate.

- Subject: "5 Ramadan recipes ready in 20 minutes"
- Preview: "Including a 3-ingredient date dessert the kids will love"

### Body copy structure

A simple, reliable structure:

1. **Hook:** the first line continues the promise of the subject line.
2. **Value:** the tip, story, product benefit or news.
3. **Proof:** a testimonial, example or result (genuine).
4. **CTA:** one primary action, repeated as a button and a text link if the email is long.
5. **Sign-off:** a human name builds connection.

Write like a person talking to one reader:

- Short paragraphs (one to three sentences).
- "You" more than "we".
- Bold or bullet key points for skimmers.
- One idea per email for promotional sends; newsletters can have more sections but should still have a clear priority.

### Calls to action

- Use action-focused, specific text: "Get the template", "Book my free call", "Shop the Eid edit".
- Make buttons large enough to tap on mobile.
- Place the primary CTA early for short emails and repeat it for long ones.
- Match the landing page to the CTA exactly.

### Tone and localisation

- For Gulf audiences, consider Arabic versions and culturally appropriate imagery and timing (for example adjusting send times during Ramadan).
- For Pakistan, English, Urdu or a mix may work; test with your audience.
- Match UK vs US spelling and date formats to the audience.
- Avoid humour that does not translate across cultures.

### Worked example

A Karachi skincare brand's promotional email:

- **From:** Hira at GlowLab
- **Subject:** Your summer skin routine (3 steps)
- **Preview:** Lightweight, non-greasy and made for humid days
- **Body:** Opens with a relatable line about humidity, gives three steps with product links, includes a short customer quote (with permission), then one button: "Build my routine".
- **Sign-off:** "Hira, founder of GlowLab".

### Common mistakes

- Vague subject lines ("Newsletter #47").
- Several competing CTAs of equal weight.
- Long blocks of text with no formatting.
- Subject lines that promise something the email does not deliver.

### Hands-on: a promotional email you can adapt

```text
FROM:     Hira at GlowLab
SUBJECT:  Your summer skin routine (3 steps)
PREVIEW:  Lightweight, non-greasy and made for humid days

Hi Sana,                                   (fallback: "Hi there,")

Karachi humidity + heavy creams = that 2pm shine we all know.

Here's the 3-step routine our customers swear by:
1. Gel cleanser – removes sweat and sunscreen without drying.
2. Niacinamide serum – helps with shine and visible pores.
3. SPF 50 fluid – light enough to reapply at lunch.

"Finally a sunscreen that doesn't melt off by noon." – Amna, verified buyer

[Build my routine]                         (button → routine bundle page, UTMs on)

Free delivery on orders over PKR 3,000 until Sunday.

Hira
Founder, GlowLab

You're receiving this because you signed up at glowlab.pk. Unsubscribe | Preferences
GlowLab, [registered business address]
```

Why it works: a recognisable sender, a specific subject, a preview that adds a reason, a first line that continues the promise, scannable value, genuine proof, one primary action and an honest deadline.

### A subject-line bank to test (by formula)

| Formula | Consumer example | B2B example |
|---|---|---|
| How-to | How to keep makeup on in 40°C | How to close your books by the 5th |
| Number | 5 iftar recipes ready in 20 minutes | 3 invoice templates that get you paid faster |
| Question | Still sweating through your gym kit? | Still reconciling COD remittances by hand? |
| News | New: Arabic calligraphy course starts Monday | New: VAT report export is live |
| Benefit | Your weekend sorted: 3 day trips from Riyadh | Save 3 hours on every payroll run |
| Story | I almost quit freelancing last year | What we learned from 200 onboarding calls |

Judge tests on **clicks or revenue per recipient**, not opens (see the modern-inboxes lesson).

### Worked example 2: a B2B plain-text email

A Dubai IT-services firm tests a designed newsletter against a plain-text note from a partner:

```text
Subject: Quick question about your Microsoft 365 renewal
Hi Omar,
Many of our clients renew Microsoft 365 licences in Q4 and overpay for seats
nobody uses. We built a 10-minute licence check – it usually finds 10-20% of seats
to remove (based on our client reviews this year).
Would a quick check before your renewal be useful? Just reply "yes" and I'll send a slot.
Faisal, Partner, [firm]
```

The plain-text version earns more replies, and replies are also a positive deliverability signal. (Any figures you quote must be real and supportable.)

### How to measure success

- Click rate and revenue (or replies) per recipient by email, compared with your recent average.
- Unsubscribe and complaint rates stay low when you change tone or frequency.
- A growing swipe file of winning subject lines, openings and CTAs with their test results.

lessons.title: Design for mobile and accessibility
lessons.body:
### Most email is read on phones A large share of emails are opened on mobile devices, often on small screens, in bright light or on slow connections. Design for mobile first, then check desktop. ### Layout principles - **Single-column layouts** are easiest to read on mobile. - **Width:** most email templates are around 600–640 pixels wide on desktop and scale down on mobile. - **Visual hierarchy:** headline, short supporting text, one prominent button, then secondary content. - **White space:** give elements room; cramped emails feel overwhelming. - **Tap targets:** buttons at least around 44 × 44 pixels, with space between links. - **Font size:** body text roughly 14–16 pixels or larger; headings larger still. ### Images - Many email clients block images by default until the reader allows them. Emails must still make sense with images off. - Always add **alt text** to images, describing content or function ("Summer skincare routine: cleanser, serum, SPF"). - Avoid **image-only emails**; put key messages and CTAs in live text and buttons (bulletproof buttons built in HTML/CSS rather than pictures of buttons). - Compress images so emails load quickly on mobile data. - Use GIFs sparingly and avoid rapid flashing. ### Accessibility checklist Accessible emails reach more people and usually perform better for everyone. - **Colour contrast:** text must stand out clearly from its background (WCAG guidance recommends a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text). - **Do not rely on colour alone** to convey meaning (for example sale prices in red only). - **Descriptive link text:** "Read the pricing guide" rather than "click here". - **Logical reading order** in the HTML so screen readers read content in the right sequence. - **Language attribute** set (for example English or Arabic) so screen readers pronounce correctly. - **Right-to-left support** for Arabic and Urdu emails: test that text direction, alignment and punctuation display correctly across major clients. - **Semantic headings** where your email builder supports them. - **Plain-text version** available. ### Dark mode Many readers use dark mode, which can invert or adjust colours. Test your emails in dark mode: - Use logos with transparent backgrounds or a subtle outline so they remain visible. - Avoid text baked into images with light backgrounds. - Check that brand colours still meet contrast requirements. ### Branding and templates Create a small set of reusable templates: - **Newsletter** (multiple sections). - **Promotional** (hero, offer, CTA). - **Plain-text style** (looks like a personal note; often works well for founder messages, B2B and re-engagement). - **Transactional** (order confirmations, receipts – clear and functional). Plain-text-style emails can outperform heavily designed ones for some audiences because they feel personal. Test both. ### Footer essentials Every marketing email footer should include: - An easy-to-find **unsubscribe link** (and preference centre). - Your **business name and postal address** (legally required under CAN-SPAM for commercial email and good practice everywhere). - A reminder of why the person is receiving the email ("You're receiving this because you signed up at…"). - Links to your privacy notice and contact details. ### Testing before sending - Send test emails to yourself on different devices and clients (Gmail app, Apple Mail, Outlook). - Use preview tools (many email platforms include them, and dedicated tools such as Litmus or Email on Acid exist). - Check all links, merge tags and fallbacks. - Check images-off and dark-mode views. - Read on a phone in daylight. ### Common mistakes - Image-only emails with no alt text. - Tiny text and cramped links on mobile. - Low-contrast brand colours. - Arabic text displaying left-to-right or broken. ### Hands-on: code patterns that make emails robust Most email builders generate this for you, but knowing the patterns helps you check the output. **A "bulletproof" button (live text, works with images off):** ```html
Build my routine
``` **Language, direction and dark-mode hints in the document head (Arabic example):** ```html ``` Support for dark-mode CSS varies by email client; always test. For mixed Arabic/English content, set `dir` on the specific blocks as well, and test punctuation and numbers. ### Size and clipping Gmail clips messages whose HTML exceeds about **102 KB**, hiding the rest behind "View entire message" – which can hide your unsubscribe link and tracking pixel. Keep HTML lean: avoid pasting from word processors, remove unused CSS and host images rather than embedding them. ### Accessibility quick test (10 minutes) 1. Turn images off – does the email still make sense and show the CTA? 2. Check contrast of body text and buttons with a contrast checker (aim for at least 4.5:1 for normal text). 3. Read the email with a screen reader (VoiceOver on iPhone or Mac, TalkBack on Android, Narrator on Windows) – is the order logical and are links descriptive? 4. Zoom to 200% on desktop – does the layout still work? 5. Check `lang` and `dir` for Arabic or Urdu versions. ### Worked example 2: a Riyadh retailer's bilingual template A Riyadh home-goods retailer rebuilds its template as a single column with two language blocks (Arabic first, right-to-left; English second, left-to-right), live-text headlines, bulletproof buttons in each language, alt text in both languages, and a dark-mode-safe logo with a transparent background and light outline. Testing across Gmail, Apple Mail and Outlook shows correct alignment and readable buttons in dark mode. Click rate on mobile rises, and customer-service emails about "blank" emails stop. ### How to measure success - Every campaign passes the images-off, dark-mode and screen-reader checks before sending. - Mobile click rate is at least as high as desktop click rate. - No clipped emails in Gmail (HTML under ~100 KB).

lessons.title: AI-assisted email: faster drafts, smarter targeting, honest messages
lessons.body:
### Where AI fits in an email programme

AI now appears in three places:

1. **General assistants** (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot) – drafting, rewriting, translating, brainstorming subject lines, summarising performance data.
2. **Features inside email platforms** – most major platforms (for example Klaviyo, Mailchimp, HubSpot and Brevo) offer AI tools for subject lines and copy, segment building from plain-language descriptions, send-time optimisation and **predictive analytics** such as expected next order date, predicted lifetime value or churn risk. Names and availability change – check your platform's current features and plan.
3. **AI in the inbox** – summaries and prioritisation by Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail (covered in the modern-inboxes lesson).

Used well, AI shortens production time and helps you personalise at scale. Used carelessly, it produces generic, inaccurate or off-brand emails – and can leak customer data.

### Good uses and human checkpoints

| Use | Where AI helps | Human checkpoint |
|---|---|---|
| Subject lines and preview text | 20–30 options across formulas | Choose; remove anything misleading; test on clicks/revenue |
| Flow copy (welcome, cart, win-back) | First drafts in your brand voice | Facts, offers, legal wording, tone |
| Translation and localisation | First pass into Arabic, Urdu or English variants | Native-speaker review, RTL layout check |
| Segments and predictions | Suggested segments; predicted next order or churn risk | Sense-check with real data; avoid sensitive inferences |
| Product recommendations | Personalised blocks | Stock, pricing, appropriateness |
| Reporting | Draft commentary from aggregated results | Verify every number; remove invented reasons |

### Hands-on: a brand-voice guide the AI can follow

Create a short voice guide once and paste it into every prompt (or save it as custom instructions or a project in your assistant):

```text
BRAND VOICE – GlowLab (skincare, Pakistan)
Audience: women 20-40 in Karachi/Lahore; practical, busy, value-conscious
Tone: warm, direct, lightly humorous; never preachy; no fear-based beauty claims
Language: simple English; Roman Urdu phrases OK in subject lines (max 1)
We say: "routine", "humid days", "shine", "gentle"
We never say: "flawless", "anti-ageing miracle", "clinically proven" (no study),
             "cure", anything about body shape or weight
Proof we may use: 4.7/5 from 1,200+ site reviews; dermatologist-reviewed formulas
Offers: free delivery over PKR 3,000; no more than 15% off except Eid/11.11
Format: short paragraphs, one CTA, sign-off "Hira, founder"
```

### Hands-on: generating a flow with guardrails

```text
Using the BRAND VOICE above, draft a 3-email abandoned-cart flow.
Timing: 2 hours, 24 hours, 72 hours after abandonment.
Email 1: friendly reminder with the cart items ({{cart_items}} merge tag) and a
         direct link back; no discount.
Email 2: reassurance: reviews, delivery times, returns, cash on delivery.
Email 3: optional incentive (free delivery only) or real low-stock message
         (use only if {{low_stock}} is true).
For each email give: subject (max 45 chars), preview (max 80 chars), body
(max 120 words), CTA text. Use ONLY the proof and offers in the voice guide.
Mark any claim that needs checking with [CHECK]. Do not invent reviews.
```

Then paste the drafts into your email platform, replace merge tags with the platform's own syntax and run the QA checklist below.

### QA checklist for AI-assisted emails

```text
[ ] Every fact, price, date and claim checked against a source
[ ] No invented testimonials, reviews, statistics or "customers"
[ ] Offers match the discount policy and landing page
[ ] Merge tags and fallbacks tested ("Hi there" when first name is missing)
[ ] Tone matches the voice guide; native-speaker check for translations
[ ] No sensitive inferences (health, pregnancy, religion, finances) in targeting or copy
[ ] No customer personal data pasted into unapproved AI tools
[ ] If an AI assistant answers replies or chats, customers are told they are talking to AI
```

### Disclosure and privacy

- **Drafting copy with AI** generally needs no special label – you remain responsible for accuracy, like any copy.
- **Synthetic people, voices or testimonials** must never be presented as real customers (the FTC's rule on fake reviews and testimonials in the US; misleading-advertising rules in the UK, EU and Gulf).

lessons.title: Welcome and nurture flows
lessons.body:
### Why automations matter

**Automations** (also called flows or journeys) are emails sent automatically when someone takes an action or reaches a condition: signing up, browsing, buying, going quiet. Because they are triggered by behaviour, they are timely and relevant, and they often generate a disproportionate share of email revenue relative to their volume. Build them once, then improve them over time.

### The welcome flow

The welcome flow is usually the most important automation. New subscribers are at peak interest; this is your chance to set expectations and build trust.

A typical e-commerce welcome flow:

| Email | Timing | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Immediately | Deliver the promised lead magnet or code; say what to expect and how often |
| 2 | Day 2 | Brand story: who you are, why you exist, what makes you different |
| 3 | Day 4 | Social proof: best-sellers, reviews, customer photos (with permission) |
| 4 | Day 6 | Education: how to choose, use or get the most from your product |
| 5 | Day 8 | Reminder of the offer before it expires (if there is one) |

A creator or B2B service welcome flow might replace product emails with best content, a case study and an invitation to reply ("What is your biggest challenge with…?"). Replies are strong positive signals for deliverability and a source of customer insight.

### Flow logic essentials

- **Trigger:** what starts the flow (joined a list, submitted a form, tagged via quiz).
- **Delays:** time between emails.
- **Conditional splits:** different paths based on behaviour or data (for example "has purchased?" → exit the discount emails).
- **Exit conditions / goals:** remove people when they achieve the goal (purchase, booking) so they do not receive irrelevant emails.
- **Filters:** exclude people who should not receive the flow (existing customers from a first-purchase offer).
- **Frequency protection:** avoid sending a flow email and a campaign on the same day where possible (smart sending features help).

### Nurture flows for leads

For higher-consideration purchases (courses, B2B services, coaching, real estate), a **nurture sequence** builds trust over weeks:

1. **Problem education:** help them understand the problem more deeply.
2. **Framework or method:** share your approach.
3. **Case study:** show a real (permitted) result.
4. **Objection handling:** price, time, fit, trust.
5. **Invitation:** book a call, start a trial, join a webinar.
6. **Follow-up:** a helpful check-in, not pressure.

Segment nurture paths by interest or lead source when possible. A lead who downloaded "SEO basics" needs different content from one who requested a pricing quote.

### Worked example: a UK online yoga studio

- **Trigger:** sign-up for a free class.
- **Email 1 (instant):** class link, what to prepare, a welcome from the instructor.
- **Email 2 (after class):** "How did it feel?" with a two-question reply prompt and a beginner programme link.
- **Split:** attended vs did not attend (from the booking system).
  - Attended: testimonials, then an introductory membership offer.
  - Did not attend: a friendly reschedule option.
- **Exit:** anyone who buys a membership moves to the member onboarding flow.

### Measuring flows

- **Revenue or conversions per recipient** for the whole flow and each email.
- **Click rate** per email.
- **Unsubscribe and complaint rates** (a spike at a specific email signals a problem).
- **Time to conversion** after entering the flow.

Review flows at least quarterly: refresh content, test subject lines and check links and offers still work.

### Common mistakes

- No welcome email, or a welcome sent days later.
- Flows without exit conditions (customers receiving "complete your first purchase" emails).
- Set-and-forget flows with broken links or expired offers.
- Discount-heavy welcome flows that train subscribers to wait for codes.

### Hands-on: a complete welcome flow with copy (e-commerce)

Adapt the brand details; keep the structure. Merge tags vary by platform – `{{ first_name|default:"there" }}` is shown as an example of a fallback.

```text
TRIGGER: joined list (confirmed)   FILTER: has not placed an order
EXIT: places an order (move to post-purchase flow)   SMART SENDING: on

EMAIL 1 – immediately
Subject: Your 10% code is inside (and what to expect)
Preview: Plus the 3 products our customers reorder most
Body:   Hi {{ first_name|default:"there" }}, welcome to Leaf & Loom.
        Here's your code: WELCOME10 (valid 7 days on your first order).
        What to expect: one email a week - new arrivals, care tips and the
        occasional offer. You can change this anytime.
        [Shop bestsellers]
        Sana, Leaf & Loom

EMAIL 2 – day 2
Subject: Why we started Leaf & Loom
Preview: A short story about linen, Lahore and doing things properly
Body:   Our story in 120 words: who we are, how we source, what makes us different.
        Photo of the workshop (alt text). [See how it's made]

EMAIL 3 – day 4
Subject: 1,200 customers, one favourite
Preview: The kurta that keeps selling out (real reviews inside)
Body:   Best-seller + 3 short, genuine reviews (with permission). [Shop the favourite]

EMAIL 4 – day 6
Subject: How to choose your size (without the guesswork)
Preview: Our 30-second fit guide + free exchanges
Body:   Fit guide, fabric care, delivery times, exchange policy, COD if offered.
        [Find my size]

EMAIL 5 – day 7 (only if code unused)
Subject: Your welcome code ends tonight
Preview: 10% off your first order until midnight
Body:   Honest reminder of the real deadline + best-sellers. [Use my code]
```

### Hands-on: a B2B nurture outline with a reply prompt

```text
TRIGGER: downloaded "VAT checklist for UAE freelancers"   EXIT: books a call
E1 (instant): the checklist + "Reply and tell me your biggest VAT headache"
E2 (day 3):   the 3 mistakes we see most (education)
E3 (day 7):   our method in 4 steps (framework)
E4 (day 11):  case study - a Dubai designer's first VAT return (with permission)
E5 (day 15):  objections: cost, time, "can I do it myself?"
E6 (day 19):  invitation: 20-minute call [Book a time]
SPLIT after E3: clicked pricing page? -> send E6 next
```

### Worked example 2: a Riyadh online course creator

A creator selling an Arabic-language design course runs a bilingual welcome flow triggered by a free mini-lesson sign-up. A conditional split by preferred language sends Arabic or English versions. Email 1 delivers the lesson; email 3 shows a student project (with permission); email 5 invites people to a live Q&A. Replies to email 1 ("What do you want to design?") are tagged in the platform and used to recommend the right course tier. Enrolment rate from the flow is tracked per language.

### How to measure success (with formulas)

- **Flow revenue per recipient** = revenue attributed to the flow ÷ people who entered it.
- **Per-email click rate** = unique clicks ÷ delivered, to find the weak email.
- **Conversion rate within 14 days** = entrants who purchased (or booked) within 14 days ÷ entrants.
- **Unsubscribe and complaint rate per email** – a spike marks the email to fix.
- For a clean read on impact, hold out a small random share (for example 10%) who receive no welcome flow and compare their 30-day conversion (see the testing lesson).

lessons.title: Abandoned cart, post-purchase and win-back flows
lessons.body:
### Recovering intent

Many shoppers add items to a cart or browse products and leave. Some were comparing prices, some were interrupted, some had doubts. **Behaviour-triggered flows** remind and reassure them. These flows require tracking of on-site behaviour with the right consent and a known email address (for example from a logged-in account, a previous click or checkout entry).

### Abandoned cart flow

| Email | Timing (typical starting point) | Content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1–4 hours after abandonment | Friendly reminder with product image, name, price and a direct link back to the cart |
| 2 | About 24 hours | Address objections: reviews, delivery times, returns policy, payment options (for example cash on delivery, instalments) |
| 3 | 48–72 hours | Optional incentive (free delivery or a small discount) or urgency based on real stock levels |

Tips:

- Do not lead with a discount; many people complete purchases with a reminder alone, and automatic discounts can train people to abandon carts.
- Exit the flow immediately when the person purchases.
- Show the exact items and make returning to the cart one tap.
- For COD-heavy markets such as Pakistan, remind shoppers that COD is available if it is.
- Consider WhatsApp or SMS reminders only for customers who opted in to those channels.

### Browse abandonment

Triggered when a known subscriber views products without adding to cart. Keep it light: "Still thinking about the linen kurta?" with the product, alternatives and reviews. Send fewer emails than cart abandonment because intent is lower.

### Post-purchase flow

The period after purchase shapes whether customers come back.

1. **Order confirmation** (transactional – clear details, delivery estimate).
2. **Shipping updates** (transactional).
3. **Onboarding or how-to-use** email: tips to get value quickly, reducing returns.
4. **Review request** after the customer has had time to use the product.
5. **Cross-sell or replenishment** based on what they bought (for example a refill reminder timed to the product's typical usage cycle).
6. **Loyalty or referral** invitation.

Keep transactional emails primarily transactional. Adding heavy promotional content to them may change their legal classification and annoy customers.

### Win-back and re-engagement

Two related but different flows:

- **Customer win-back:** customers who have not purchased for longer than your typical purchase cycle. Example: a customer who usually reorders coffee every 6 weeks but has not ordered for 12 weeks.
- **Subscriber re-engagement:** subscribers who have not clicked for many months (part of your sunset policy).

A win-back sequence might be:

1. "We miss you" with what is new since their last purchase.
2. A personalised recommendation or incentive.
3. Feedback request: "Was something wrong?" with a short survey.
4. Final message: "Should we stop emailing?" with a clear option to stay subscribed.

Suppress re-engagement non-responders to protect deliverability. They can always return.

### Timing and discount strategy

Illustrative starting timings are guides only. Test them against your own buying cycle. Decide your **discount policy** in advance:

- Which flows may offer incentives.
- Maximum discount levels that protect margin (remember break-even ROAS and margin from earlier courses).
- Unique, single-use codes to prevent sharing on coupon sites.

### Worked example (illustrative)

A Riyadh coffee subscription brand builds:

- **Abandoned cart:** reminder at 2 hours, reviews and free delivery threshold at 24 hours, no discount.
- **Post-purchase:** brewing guide on day 3, review request on day 10, replenishment reminder on day 35.
- **Win-back:** at 10 weeks without an order, "New single-origin beans are here", then a 10% single-use code, then a feedback survey.

The team tracks revenue per recipient for each flow and tests timing each quarter.

### Common mistakes

- Offering the biggest discount in the first reminder.
- Not exiting people who have purchased.
- Review requests before the product has arrived.
- Keeping inactive subscribers forever instead of re-engaging or suppressing.

### Hands-on: abandoned cart copy (3 emails)

```text
TRIGGER: started checkout, no order within 1 hour   EXIT: places order
FILTER: not already in flow in last 14 days; marketing consent (where required)

EMAIL 1 – 2 hours
Subject: You left something in your cart
Preview: We've saved it for you - pick up where you left off
Body:   {{ cart item image, name, size, price }}
        Your cart is saved. [Return to my cart]
        Questions about size or delivery? Just reply - a real person answers.

EMAIL 2 – 24 hours
Subject: Still deciding? Here's what others say
Preview: 4.7/5 from 1,200+ reviews, easy exchanges, cash on delivery
Body:   2 short genuine reviews of the item (or the brand)
        Delivery: 2-4 working days - Exchanges: 14 days - COD available
        [Complete my order]

EMAIL 3 – 72 hours (optional incentive)
Subject: Free delivery on your order - today only
Preview: Your cart is still waiting (items may sell out)
Body:   Free delivery if you complete your order by midnight (single-use code: FREEDEL-{{code}}).
        Mention low stock ONLY if true for an item in the cart. [Use free delivery]
```

### Hands-on: post-purchase and win-back copy

```text
POST-PURCHASE
Day 3 (after delivery): "Getting the best from your linen kurta" - care tips, styling ideas.
Day 10: Subject "How's the fit?" - one-click star rating + short review form.
Day 30-45: cross-sell or replenishment based on the item (timed to the usage cycle).

WIN-BACK (customers past their usual reorder gap)
E1 Subject: It's been a while - here's what's new
   Body: 3 new arrivals chosen from their past category. [See what's new]
E2 Subject: A little thank-you for coming back
   Body: single-use 10% code, 7 days (within discount policy). [Shop with my code]
E3 Subject: Was it something we did?
   Body: 2-question survey (what changed? what would bring you back?) + preference centre.
EXIT: purchase. After E3 with no response: move to regular cadence or sunset rules.
```

### Hands-on: setting a discount ceiling from your margins

Before any incentive, calculate the most you can give away and still earn your target contribution per order:

```text
Maximum discount % = Contribution margin % - Target contribution margin % after discount

Example: contribution margin 45%, you want at least 30% left after the incentive
-> maximum discount ≈ 15% of the order value (or a free-delivery cost below that)
```

Prefer non-price incentives (free delivery, a gift with purchase, an extended exchange window) when they cost you less than a percentage discount.

### Worked example 2: a UK furniture retailer

A Leeds furniture retailer's carts average £900 and customers compare for days. The team extends the timing (4 hours, 2 days, 5 days), replaces discounts with **free fabric swatches** and **finance options** (where regulated and properly disclosed), and adds a "book a showroom visit" option. Cart recovery revenue per recipient rises and discount costs fall to zero.

### How to measure success

- **Cart flow revenue per recipient** and **recovery rate** (orders from the flow ÷ carts entering it).
- **Discount cost per recovered order** – should fall as reminders do more of the work.
- **Win-back reactivation rate** (lapsed customers who order within 30 days of entering) and survey insights.
- A small holdout on the cart flow to confirm the recovered orders are incremental.
